An algorithm is a step-by-step computational procedure that transforms input data into output and is guaranteed to terminate. Every program is ultimately an algorithm, and every algorithm can be analyzed for correctness, efficiency, and scalability. Algorithms exist independent of any programming language. The same algorithm can be implemented in Python, C++, or Rust with identical logic.

An algorithm must have three properties. It must be finite, terminating in a bounded number of steps. It must be deterministic, meaning the same input always produces the same output. And it must be well-defined, so each step is unambiguous. Correctness means the algorithm actually solves the stated problem. Efficiency means it does so with minimal time and space.

Algorithms fall into classic categories. Search algorithms locate items in data, like linear search and binary search. Sorting algorithms order sequences—quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort are the canonical examples. Graph algorithms traverse or optimize networks. BFS and DFS explore graphs. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths. String matching finds substrings in text.

Complexity analysis uses Big O notation to formalize how runtime grows. O of one means constant time. O of n is linear. O of n squared is quadratic. Exponential growth is O of two to the n. For any algorithm, there's a best case, a worst case, and an average case. These describe performance under different input distributions. Algorithms always have trade-offs. Some are fast but use a lot of memory. Others save space at the cost of time.

Fundamental techniques structure algorithm design. Brute force tries all possibilities exhaustively. It's often slow but sometimes necessary. Divide and conquer breaks the problem into independent subproblems, solves each one, and merges the results. Dynamic programming caches results from subproblems to avoid redundant computation. Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices, hoping that leads to global optimality.

Understanding algorithms deeply is central to computer science. Every practical problem boils down to choosing the right algorithm. Routing data through a network, compressing video, predicting weather, sorting millions of records—all require algorithmic thinking. Moving from an O of n squared to O of n log n sorting algorithm can mean the difference between a program that runs in seconds versus hours. Understanding algorithms teaches you to think about problems abstractly before committing to code. That skill transfers across all programming domains. Algorithms connect directly to recursion, since many elegant algorithms exploit recursive structure. Divide and conquer is a systematic algorithm design paradigm. Greedy algorithms are one class of algorithmic strategy with well-known trade-offs. Graph algorithms solve routing, scheduling, and matching problems. And Big O notation is the formal language for algorithm analysis.
